item.title: NFL news, live updates: Colts trade Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson to Seahawks, send DeForest Buckner to 49ers in reunion
item.description: Follow along with the latest NFL news ahead of Week 8.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to Week 8, where the rumor mill continues to heat up as we continue to inch closer to the NFL’s trade deadline on Nov. 10 at 4 p.m. ET.

After falling to 2-5 with a loss against the Minnesota Vikings, the Indianapolis Colts appear to have started the “fire sale,” sending Pro Bowl guard Quenten Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks in a trade to shore up some protection for Sam Darnold. The Colts are without their first-round pick in 2027 after trading it to the New York Jets in exchange for All-Pro cornerback Sauce Gardner, so we’ll be on the lookout for more potential trades in an effort to increase their draft capital amidst a rebuild.

Follow along with Yahoo Sports for the latest NFL news, trade rumors, injury updates and more ahead of Week 8.

item.title: Cowboys rookie report: Quieter roles in much-needed win over Philadelphia
item.description: What do you make of the Cowboys rookie class so far this season?
item.content:encoded:
Dallas got the result it needed on Monday night, beating Philadelphia 38–21 to move to 3–4. The veterans supplied the biggest moments, while the rookie class had a quieter evening. Jaishawn Barham’s workload dropped, Caleb Downs had tackling issues to clean up, and Camden Brown finally made his NFL debut. 

But here is how each rookie fared this week, listed in draft order, and any undrafted players worth noting after that. 

Caleb Downs

(56 defensive snaps | 5 tackles | 0 TFL | 0 sacks | 0 INT | 0 passes defended | 0 pressures | 0 QB hits)

Downs contributed three solo tackles, two assists, and was credited with one run stop. The concern was finishing where he was also charged with two missed tackles against the run. There was useful involvement, but those missed opportunities kept this from being a clean performance.

Malachi Lawrence

(30 defensive snaps | 1 tackle | 0 TFL | 0 sacks | 0 INT | 0 passes defended | 0 QB hits)

Lawrence contributed a run stop, although the box score recorded his tackle as an assist. His impact remained modest, with no sacks or quarterback hits. Dallas got its two sacks from Quinnen Williams and Donovan Ezeiruaku, meaning Lawrence still needs to turn his opportunities into more decisive plays. 

Jaishawn Barham

(21 defensive snaps | 2 tackles | 0 TFL | 0 sacks | 0 INT | 0 passes defended | 0 pressures | 0 QB hits)

Barham played a smaller role with DeMarvion Overshown back, while Shemar James also received substantial playing time. Barham was also charged with one completion for 12 yards on two targets. He avoided a costly coverage total, but two tackles and no disruptive plays made this a quiet contribution.

LT Overton

(23 defensive snaps | 1 tackle | 0 TFL | 0 sacks | 0 INT | 0 passes defended | 1 pressure | 0 QB hits)

Overton supplied one pressure across 16 pass-rush snaps, giving Dallas a little disruption from its rotation. His only tackle was an assist, and he did not produce a stop behind the line. He was also charged with a critical penalty near the goal line. There was a contribution, but limited production overall.

Camden Brown

(4 ST snaps | 0 targets | 0 receptions | 0 receiving yards | 0 TD)

Brown finally made his regular-season debut after being inactive through the opening six games. His opportunity came entirely on special teams, so there was no receiving performance to judge. Getting onto the field was a first step, earning offensive work is the next challenge.

item.title: All-22 Review: How Quenton Nelson can transform the Seahawks offensive line
item.description: Seattle acquired the six-time All-Pro to improve Sam Darnold’s protection and bring much-needed consistency to the run game. The film shows why Seattle got him.
item.content:encoded:
John Schneider has never been particularly hesitant to pursue veteran help when he believes a roster is close to contending. The Seattle Seahawks’ acquisition of Quenton Nelson from the Indianapolis Colts is the latest example, and it addresses one of the team’s most pressing needs without costing a first- or second-round draft pick.

Seattle sent Indianapolis a third-round selection in 2027 and a fifth-rounder in 2028, while taking on approximately $9.777 million in prorated salary for the remainder of Nelson’s 2026 contract. For a team sitting at 4-3 and hoping to make a serious postseason run, the move is a clear attempt to improve an offense that hasn’t consistently delivered.

The rationale is straightforward. Seattle needs to give Sam Darnold a cleaner pocket and create more room for its running backs. Nelson has spent much of his career doing both at an exceptionally high level. The question isn’t whether his résumé justifies the move; it’s whether his current form can help Seattle overcome the problems that have held the offense back this season.

At 30, Nelson already has six All-Pro selections and eight consecutive Pro Bowl appearances to begin his career. According to the Elias Sports Bureau, since the AFL-NFL merger in 1970, only four offensive players have made the Pro Bowl in each of their first eight seasons: Nelson, Hall of Fame running backs Franco Harris and Barry Sanders, and offensive tackle Joe Thomas.

That is an extraordinary group to join. Seattle isn’t acquiring a developmental prospect or trying to rehabilitate a player who has fallen out of favor. It is bringing in a veteran whose track record suggests he can still be a difference-maker at one of the most physically demanding positions on the field.

A 2018 Draft Connection Comes Full Circle

Nelson’s arrival also creates an unexpected connection with Seattle’s quarterback.

In the 2018 NFL Draft, the New York Jets moved from No. 6 to No. 3 overall to select USC quarterback Sam Darnold. The Colts remained at No. 6 and selected Nelson.

The price for New York was substantial: the sixth overall pick, two second-round selections in 2018 and another second-rounder in 2019. The Jets used the third pick on Darnold, while Indianapolis landed the offensive lineman who would become one of the defining players of his position.

Eight years later, those two careers intersect again in Seattle. The Seahawks are hoping Nelson can help create the conditions for Darnold to operate more effectively, particularly by limiting interior pressure and giving the running game a more reliable foundation.

Why the Seahawks needed help inside

The Seahawks’ offensive struggles have been reflected in several underlying metrics, and the run game has been especially concerning. Seattle ranked last in the NFL in yards before contact on runs designed through the B gaps, averaging just 0.3 yards per attempt, 0.5 yards less than 31st.

The broader picture is equally troubling. Seattle ranked 26th in offensive EPA per play, 31st in EPA per designed run and 27th in run-block win rate. Its running backs averaged 3.6 yards per designed run, good for 28th in the league, while the team also ranked 28th in yards before contact on designed runs. Pass-block win rate placed the Seahawks 21st.

No single statistic explains every problem, but together they point toward an offensive line that hasn’t consistently won its assignments. When the interior fails to establish leverage or create movement, running backs are forced to make decisions before reaching the line of scrimmage. In pass protection, losses up front allow defenders to collapse the pocket and shorten Darnold’s decision-making window.

Nelson’s skill set directly addresses those concerns. His combination of power, hand placement and leverage has made him a particularly effective interior blocker, capable of creating movement at the point of attack while maintaining control of his assignment.

There is evidence that his pass protection can still be a strength. Through Week 7, Nelson had logged 275 pass-blocking snaps without allowing a sack, with a reported pressure rate allowed of 2.2% in one statistical breakdown.

His overall numbers, however, deserve closer attention. ESPN’s win-rate data placed Nelson in the 66th percentile in pass protection and the 37th percentile in run blocking in 2026. Those figures are below his marks in the previous two seasons, particularly as a run blocker.

That doesn’t necessarily mean his best football is behind him. Nelson experienced a dip in 2022 and 2023 before returning to an elite level in 2024 and delivering another strong season in 2025. Seattle will be betting that the player who reestablished himself among the league’s best can bring that level of performance to a line that badly needs it.

Joe Thuney offers a useful point of comparison. The Chiefs signed Thuney in 2021, when he was around the age Nelson is now. After arriving in Kansas City, Thuney earned three consecutive first-team All-Pro selections. Nelson could provide a similar boost, particularly if Seattle can work out an extension and keep him in the lineup beyond this season.

The trade cost is manageable. The next contract….

The draft compensation is relatively modest for a player with Nelson’s credentials. Seattle gave up a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick, then assumed approximately $9.777 million of his remaining 2026 salary obligation.

The larger financial decision may come after the season. Nelson is approaching the end of his current contract, and acquiring him could be only the first step if Seattle wants to keep him in the lineup long term.

The guard market offers a useful reference point. Peter Skoronski’s deal averages $25 million per year, followed by Trey Smith at $23.5 million and Chris Lindstrom at $21.8 million. At center, Tyler Linderbaum’s reported annual value is $27 million, while Creed Humphrey’s is $18 million.

Given Nelson’s résumé, an extension approaching +$25 million annually would not be surprising. Schneider has made several notable in-season acquisitions over the years, including LT Duane Brown in 2017, S Quandre Diggs in 2019, EDGE Carlos Dunlap in 2020, DL Leonard Williams in 2023, LB Ernest Jones IV in 2024 and WR/KR Rashid Shaheed in 2025.

Those trades haven’t always come with an immediate contract extension. Seattle can take a similar approach with Nelson, using the remainder of 2026 to evaluate his performance before deciding how much to invest in his future. The new deals for Ernest Jones IV and Leonard Williams turned out to be strong values, while the price Seattle paid to retain Rashid Shaheed felt like an overpay. Nelson presents another test of Schneider’s ability to balance immediate impact with long-term value. Whether the Seahawks can keep him beyond this season—and at what price—will be just as important as what he delivers on the field.

How Quenton Nelson fits into Seattle’s starting line

The most straightforward lineup adjustment would be to put Nelson at his established position of left guard and move Grey Zabel to right guard. That would allow Nelson to operate on the side where he has built his reputation while giving Seattle a chance to improve the interior without completely rebuilding the offensive line.

Anthony Bradford, who recently returned from injured reserve, would be the most likely candidate to lose his starting spot under that arrangement.

Zabel’s versatility makes the switch possible, but his experience on the right side should not be overstated. He played just three games on RG during his time at North Dakota State. His work at multiple positions during Senior Bowl practices demonstrated an ability to learn different assignments, although practice experience is not the same as an established track record in a particular role.

Moving Zabel to center appears less likely. The position requires more than the ability to block one-on-one: the center must deliver the snap consistently and help communicate protections and adjustments before the play. Unless Seattle sees a compelling reason to make that change, keeping Zabel at guard is the more natural solution.

The final configuration will depend on how the coaching staff evaluates the combinations, but the likely goal is clear: put Nelson in a position to play to his strengths while allowing Zabel to develop without taking on more responsibility than necessary.

What Quenton Nelson Adds: All-22 Review

Nelson’s talent is nothing new. It was evident in college, when he became one of the highest-drafted guards in NFL history and entered an exclusive group. Since 1985, only three guards have been selected among the first six overall picks in the NFL Draft: Bill Fralic, taken second by the Atlanta Falcons in 1985; Brandon Scherff, selected fifth by Washington in 2015; and Nelson, drafted sixth overall by the Colts in 2018.

Here’s a matchup we should see several times over the next few years: Myles Garrett against Quenton Nelson. Two outstanding players. Hopefully, this is the result we see consistently.

Nelson’s technique is outstanding. His execution is firm and precise, leaving the defender with virtually no time to react. It’s a rare level of technical ability.

Even at 30, Nelson can neutralize second-level defenders with excellent angles. He also consistently finishes blocks by putting opponents on the ground. He’s an excellent addition to a zone-running scheme.

Another snap, another defender on the ground. Nelson uses excellent technique and takes the right angle to open the cutback lane for the running back, allowing the play to develop into a solid gain.

Seattle’s offensive line has struggled with technique and communication on these types of blocks, occasionally allowing linebackers to run untouched into the backfield. Nelson should be a significant upgrade in that area.

Nelson combines technique with power to move defensive linemen and control the line of scrimmage. Seattle has repeatedly struggled to create running lanes through physical dominance, and this may be the area where Nelson can make the most immediate difference.

If you ever need to explain the concept of a reach block, this is a good example.

A reach block is an attempt by an offensive lineman to get across the face of a defender aligned to the outside, using lateral movement to reach a position in front of him and seal off his path. It’s common in outside zone schemes, where the offensive line must control horizontal space.

Unlike a drive block, the goal isn’t necessarily to push the defender backward. The priority is winning the positioning battle and preventing the defender from crossing the block to pursue the running back. If the defender wins that battle, he can penetrate the backfield and disrupt the run. It’s one of the more demanding blocks in football, requiring both precise technique and considerable athletic ability.

This is pin-and-pull executed properly. Nelson pulls into the space created by the blocking scheme. Watch how he adjusts his path to the defender’s positioning, finding the best angle to open the gap for the touchdown.

Screens are another staple of Fleury’s offense, and Nelson could be valuable in that area as well. Notice his patience: he doesn’t rush downfield, allowing the play to develop while avoiding an illegal-block penalty. He reaches the linebacker and clears the path for the running back like a snowplow.

Final Thoughts

The Seahawks have addressed one of the most pressing weaknesses on their roster by acquiring a proven difference-maker at guard. Nelson’s combination of power, technique and experience gives Seattle a chance to reshape its offensive line, improve its ground game and create a cleaner pocket for Sam Darnold. Just as importantly, his arrival gives the coaching staff more flexibility in how it builds the unit around him.

This is the kind of move that reflects Seattle’s belief in its current championship window. The challenge now is to integrate Nelson into the line, find the right combination alongside him and determine at the price that a long-term extension makes sense. If those pieces fall into place, the Seahawks could come away with far more than an immediate upgrade: they could establish a foundation for a more consistent offense.

Go Hawks!

item.title: The Good and the Bad from Chiefs’ loss in Seattle
item.description: A positive note and two learning lessons from Kansas City’s loss to the Seahawks.
item.content:encoded:
The Kansas City Chiefs lost their first game of the season in Week 7, 20-3, to the Seattle Seahawks.

Let’s look at one thing that went well and two things that didn’t from the game:

The Good

Mansoor Delane in a trail position

The Chiefs had few bright spots on offense, defense, or special teams. However, I do think rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane deserves recognition for playing a very good game overall.

Going back to his film at LSU, one of Delane’s best skills is his ability to win in trail position. Delane isn’t often behind a play, but that can happen occasionally as a cornerback, depending on your leverage.

The Chiefs are in a Cover 1 bracket here, bracketing wide receiver Jaxon-Smith Ngijba with a single-high safety. Delane is in outside leverage, with help over the middle. Delane gets about a step behind the wide receiver, but he closes that space and gets his arm in the way to break up the pass. Delane’s recovery speed is great, and he does a great job poking the ball out with late hands.

The Chiefs send a blitz this time with a Cover 2 man coverage call behind it, putting Delane in inside leverage. He recognizes that Smith-Njigba is trying to get Delane to shift outside so he can get inside positioning on the slant, but Delane sits all over it and boxes Smith-Njigba out of getting inside positioning.

Delane covered Smith-Njigba on both his go routes along the sideline, but truthfully, that wasn’t bad coverage. Smith-Njigba is the best receiver in the NFL, and Delane had to cover him one-on-one on a two-way go. Most guys get beat there. Because Smith-Njigba is so good in the middle of the field, Delane has to worry about not letting Smith-Njigba cross his face, which lets him get a step downfield. Delane is still in fine position and makes an attempt to knock the ball out; the throws and catches are just better. You’ll take this coverage every time.

The Bad

L’Jarius Sneed playing man coverage in the slot

L’Jarius Sneed was resigned this offseason to provide cornerback depth, but with the Chiefs not knowing who to start in the slot, defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo elected to go with the veteran Sneed.

Sneed started his career in the slot, and his physicality and blitzing make him well-suited to that position. Sneed played great from the slot against the Denver Broncos in Week 1, but since then, he’s been a total liability in coverage. Sneed’s snaps have also been slowly reduced, with only 14 against Seattle and almost none after halftime.

Despite only playing 14 snaps, Sneed’s play hurt the Chiefs. At this stage of his career, he can’t cover in man-to-man anymore, and Seattle knew it. The veteran allowed 83 yards over five receptions in the first half alone, according to Sumer Sports. Farzin Vousoughian on Xnoted that Sneed has also allowed the most receptions in the NFL this season and the fourth-most receiving yards (378).

The Chiefs are running a Cover 2 man coverage again, where Sneed bluffs the blitz and drops to coverage. Sneed has inside positioning on Smith-Njigba, so a slant shouldn’t be able to cross his face. But Sneed’s footwork and change of direction are much slower than they used to be, leaving him flat-footed when Smith-Njigba runs inside. He has no chance of recovering, and this turns into a first down.

Another play where Sneed is slow to click and close on a slant, and the receiver easily crosses his face. It was a theme in the loss, especially on third down; site manager Ron Kopp Jr. a few more plays where Sneed was beat earlier this week.

Sneed can’t play in the slot anymore. If he’s going to play, he has to play outside, where he has more chances to defend vertical routes. Move Delane to the slot more if necessary. I would play Chris Rolland-Wallace more, and either play Jaden Hicks in Dime over Sneed or kick Delane inside and Sneed to the boundary.

The Chiefs’ pass rush

The most frustrating part of this game was that the Chiefs pass rush did nothing against a shaky Seattle offensive line. The Chiefs finished with zero sacks and only one player hitting Darnold (defensive end George Karlaftis had two quarterback hits, per Pro Football Reference).

Watching the game back, the thing that was noticeable was that the Chiefs got no interior pressure in this game. Sam Darnold never had to throw in muddy pockets. He could step up freely to avoid R Mason Thomas and George Karlaftis off the edge.

The stats back this up. Chris Jones finished this game with zero pressures. Peter Woods had zero pressures. Khyris Tonga had one and Felix Anudike-Uzomah had two to lead their interior pass rush. The 250 lb edge player.

The issue is, this has been the case all year. Jones has 13 pressures in six games. That’s a low amount for a player like Jones. Jones only had 18 in six games to start last year and then turned it on when the season was desperate. But he hasn’t looked great this year. It looks harder for him to get upfield and turn the quick corner that he used to be great at.

Woods has also brought no juice as a pass rusher this year. He has two pressures all year and has a 2.3% pressure rate. The Chiefs put Anudike-Uzomah on the field on third downs over Woods because Woods has struggled to get any pressure.

The issue with this is the Chiefs defensive ends aren’t big enough to rush inside. Anudike-Uzomah is 250 lbs and struggles to move guards backwards. Ashton Gillotte got chances to do that in this game and it didn’t look great. You want Thomas and Karlaftis running around the edge because they are good at that. But if there isn’t any interior pressure, you allow quarterbacks to freely step into the pocket and hit receivers. The Chiefs need their defensive tackles to play better for this to be a great defense.

item.title: Seahawks swap practice squad tight ends, sign Ben Sims
item.description: It’s one in, one out at tight end to start Week 8 for the Seahawks.
item.content:encoded:
The tight end room has seen a swap to begin Week 8.

A week after the Seattle Seahawks signed veteran tight end Josiah Deguara to their practice squad, in the wake of Elijah Arroyo’s season-ending shoulder injury, they released the seven-year pro to make room for fellow tight end Ben Sims.

Sims, in his fourth season, spent training camp and preseason with the Miami Dolphins before he was placed on injured reserve and ultimately waived with an injury designation early in September.

The former Baylor Bear went undrafted in the 2023 NFL Draft, signing with the Minnesota Vikings as a UDFA. Sims was released by the Vikings ahead of his rookie campaign and signed with the Green Bay Packers, where he spent his first two seasons, playing in all 34 games, before he was released early last season. He finished the season back with the Vikings, suiting up in eight games.

Across 45 career games, Sims has caught 11 passes for 93 yards and one touchdown.

With Arroyo on injured reserve, Seattle has AJ Barner, Eric Saubert, and Nick Kallerup to call from at tight end on the 53-man roster, while Sims now rounds out the group on the practice squad.

item.title: Liam Coen: Colts traded away two good players right before we play them, can't deny that
item.description: Jaguars head coach Liam Coen acknowledged that his team's task got a little easier when the Colts traded away two of their top players, offensive lineman Quenton Nelson and defensive lineman DeForest Buckner.
item.content:encoded:
Jaguars head coach Liam Coen acknowledged that his team's task got a little easier when the Colts traded away two of their top players, offensive lineman Quenton Nelson and defensive lineman DeForest Buckner. The Jaguars face the Colts on Sunday, and now it's a Colts team that has turned its attention away from winning this year and toward building for the future.

But Coen also cautioned that the Jaguars can't allow themselves to be thinking about what's going on with the Colts.

"Obviously really good players that I have a lot of respect for. Quenton Nelson was playing some of the best football of his career, as was Buckner in a lot of ways — extremely disruptive in both the run and the pass, tipped balls, created some issues inside," Coen said. "It's two good players, you can't deny that. But knowing what that team is going to want to do, this has to all be about our improvements, us getting back on track. Got a good division opponent that we're playing at home, and the focus level, getting in pads today, has to be about our execution, our fundamentals and technique, because you can't control that stuff and if you think about it too much it typically doesn't help."

Asked if he thought the Colts might trade Jonathan Taylor, too, Coen indicated that he doesn't think that's going to happen.

"You try not to get into that world because it's just rat poison either way," Coen said. "And also a part of you wants to beat good teams, you want to beat opponents that provide strong competition, as this team does."

Coen wants his players to remember that the Colts team that shows up on Sunday will be playing to win.

"Philly a couple weeks ago had a lot of guys out and played us to the last second," Coen said. "In this league, any given Sunday, we all know anything can happen."

item.title: Making the case for and against the 49ers to go all in
item.description: The Niners could push all the chips in the next few weeks. Should they?
item.content:encoded:
At 7-1, the San Francisco 49ers are the favorites to win the Super Bowl this season, even after their first loss of the year, as they enter a needed bye week to get healthy.

Coming out of that bye week, though, and looking towards the second half of the season, their team could look different. The 49ers already traded for defensive tackle DeForest Buckner, sending a fourth-round pick to the Indianapolis Colts for the 32-year-old on an expiring contract.

And more could be coming, with the 49ers still having a few gaps to fill on their roster.

Following the 7-1 start, many have looked for San Francisco to push all the chips in for a Super Bowl this season, which would involve sending serious capital for stars. The 49ers are no stranger to trade deadline moves, although some, most notably the Christian McCaffrey trade, have had more magnitude than others.

Over the years, we’ve seen teams go all in and hurt themselves for the future, while others have taken the pieces they’ve acquired with them on a Super Bowl run.

Does it make sense for San Francisco to go all in here? Let’s make the case for both sides.

Why they should

As I mentioned at the top, the 49ers are the clear favorites to win the Super Bowl currently, followed by the Buffalo Bills, Kansas City Chiefs, Seattle Seahawks, and Los Angeles Rams.

We know the 49ers flaws, with injuries easily being the main issue. But when you look at the NFL, it’s easy to poke holes in nearly every contender. Buffalo’s defense has been a major question mark. Kansas City still doesn’t have those top-tier receiving threats, and their defense lost some key talent over the offseason. Seattle has struggled without Klint Kubiak at times offensively, and Sam Darnold has been erratic. And the Rams have just outright struggled on both sides of the ball at times.

The field is quite wide open right now. And after all the failures and miscues with reaching and winning a Super Bowl in the last few years, this could be San Francisco’s shot to do it all. If they do win the trophy, there’s no worrying talk about going all in at all.

San Francisco also has very few holes on its roster. Realistically, they could just push all their chips in on an edge rusher and call it a day. They could also go for rotational pieces that can be more complementary to their depth.

The 49ers core is getting older. This team is as well-coached as any in the country. It feels like this is the widest-open race San Francisco has been in in some time, hence the idea of going all in. Additionally, the teams underneath them will very likely make trades as well. They’ll need to respond.

Why they shouldn’t

We’ve seen teams make Hail Mary moves that have seriously backfired on them, and the 49ers could be in danger of doing the same.

The 49ers would have to part with legitimate draft capital to go all in, and that could seriously hamper them in future years. We saw the major trade back in 2021 ahead of the draft and the ramifications it had on the 49ers over the next few years with the draft.

In today’s NFL, you need young, cost-controlled talent on your roster to win a Super Bowl, and the 49ers have been doing a good job acquiring that over the last two years to put together a roster that can compete for a championship. Their formula is working.

Going all in could also hamper development, as an edge rusher takes away reps from Keion White and Mykel Williams, among others.

The 49ers have some solid 2027 draft capital with one pick in every round, although they lost a fourth in the DeForest Buckner trade. With as old a roster as they have, and as well as they’ve drafted recently, is it worth it to splurge and lose the capital?

Final Thoughts

I haven’t been a full proponent of going “all in” in years past, but this year’s case feels different for the 49ers. It truly feels like it could be their last shot at such an open title race. Contracts are only going to get more expensive, and the team’s stars are going to continue to age.

There are also inherent flaws in nearly every team around them, and the biggest competition right now comes in the AFC in terms of title odds.

An edge rusher feels like a must. Perhaps that’s all they need to do, but the 49ers have a true chance here to really separate themselves on paper, and it doesn’t have to be an expensive deadline either.

We’ve seen the 49ers draft well and construct rosters as good as any other team in the NFL. They should be able to sustain success even if they lose another draft pick or two, but it would be tough knowing they lost out on a chance for the Super Bowl in a few months because a different contender made the trade they needed to.

item.title: Jonathan Taylor trade scenarios: 5 best landing spots and what each means for fantasy football
item.description: Scott Pianowski breaks down Jonathan Taylor's fantasy outlook with five potential trade partners.
item.content:encoded:
Not long ago, an in-season trade speculation piece was basically a waste of time. NFL teams were reluctant to make deals, and when they actually occurred, it was rare for the players on the move to quickly acclimate to their new clubs. Much ado about nothing.

But things have shifted in recent years. It's helped that the trade deadline is now parked in November (it previously was slotted after Week 6). And teams seem less afraid of making mistakes now, more willing to take some chances.

This brings us to Jonathan Taylor, starting running back for the Colts. He's the center of the NFL rumor mill at the moment.

Indianapolis, of course, is off to a horrible start. The Colts sit 2-5 and even in a weak division, they're given just a 7% chance of making the playoffs, per DVOA.

The front office realizes the season is basically cooked, and Tuesday the Colts made a couple of trades. Star offensive guard Quenton Nelson was shipped to Seattle, and stalwart defensive tackle DeForest Buckner was reunited with the 49ers. The Colts landed a third and fifth-round pick for Nelson, and a fourth-round pick for Buckner. Taylor could be the next Colt to hit the trade market.

While fantasy managers paid keen attention to both deals, especially the Nelson move, a Taylor swap would be seismic in the fantasy landscape. Let's examine the prime contenders for a possible Taylor trade, and see how the pieces fit. (And while you're reading the shopping list, don't forger to add Seth McGowan, the Indianapolis backup RB, just in case.)

Minnesota Vikings

Here's a pretty clean fit. The undefeated Vikings are all defense (second in DVOA) and no offense (30th in DVOA) through their opening six games. Aaron Jones Sr. has been a decent back for a decade, but will be 32 in December. Jordan Mason isn't a bad player, but he's caught just 28 passes in his career (none this season). Taylor would immediately give the Vikings a three-down bell cow, and take some pressure off struggling QB Kyler Murray.

The Vikings likely recognize their window here. The NFC doesn't have a dominant team. The NFC East and NFC South between them might not have any good teams. The Rams have gotten off to a nightmare start. The 49ers are formidable, but battling cluster injuries. Seattle is a good but imperfect team. Even in a competitive NFC North, it's a good time for Minnesota to shove in some chips.

This would likely be a slight upgrade for Taylor. At least game flow would be improved more often than not.

Seattle Seahawks

Speaking of those imperfect Seahawks, maybe they could kick the tires on Taylor. They upgraded their running game with the Nelson move Tuesday, but the backfield is still a bunch of question marks. Emanuel Wilson is averaging just 3.6 yards per carry. Jadarian Price (chest) and Zach Charbonnet (torn ACL) recently had their practice windows opened, but they're far from guarantees. Seattle's team shape is much like Minnesota's — dominant defense, below-average offense. Taylor would instantly make the Seahawks more balanced and more dangerous.

Taylor's fantasy value would remain lofty in Seattle. This team often plays with a lead, and it seldom wants Sam Darnold to throw 40 or more passes. The offensive line now grades as a plus unit with Nelson aboard.

Denver Broncos

Here's yet another team with a defensive tilt. The Broncos are 5-2 on the strength of their No. 5 defense (per DVOA). The offense ranks just 30th in yards per game, though a difficult schedule has played into that (DVOA ranks Denver 16th on offense, which underlines how taxing the slate has been). The team is averaging just 3.8 yards per carry.

But maybe the timing for a Taylor trade isn't right here. Rookie Jonah Coleman was impressive in his Week 7 return (11 touches, 69 yards) and was a versatile back in his four-year college career. The Broncos also have veteran J.K. Dobbins and second-year back RJ Harvey, imperfect players but legitimate NFL runners. I suspect the Broncos would surely listen on a Taylor trade, but I doubt they'd do it proactively.

Green Bay Packers

The Packers might have choked up when they saw how inexpensive Nelson was in trade. Green Bay's offensive line has been screaming for help all year as one of the worst run-blocking units in the league. But a Taylor trade might complicate things, given Josh Jacobs has returned.

Taylor managers don't want their back to head to Green Bay. The blocking will be worse, the competition for the ball will be increased. I suspect the Packers are just a longshot in the Taylor sweepstakes anyway, even as they've been one of the primary teams mentioned.

Cincinnati Bengals

Here's the sleeper in the Taylor chase, a team that hasn't primarily been mentioned. But maybe that's an oversight. Cincinnati sits at 4-2, is second in the DVOA ranks, has assembled a plus offense and (for once) a credible defense. Keep Joe Burrow healthy and great things can happen.

The one disappointment in the Cincinnati offense (fantasy managers know all about it) has been Chase Brown. He's averaging just 3.5 yards per carry, and he's been nothing special as a receiver (4.3 yards per target). At his best, Brown is a solid player. Taylor at his best is a superstar. Maybe Cincinnati could get frisky in the Taylor market.

Fantasy managers would probably OK the move. If the Bengals moved for Taylor, it surely wouldn't be to make him a committee back. When Burrow, Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins are healthy, the Bengals have little trouble matriculating the ball down the field.

item.title: Several Eagles players listed among top 25 trade candidates ahead of the deadline
item.description: The Eagles could be sellers as we approach the NFL trade deadline.
item.content:encoded:
This season went sideways quickly for the Eagles, and as we approach the NFL trade deadline (Tuesday, November 10) it looks like Howie Roseman could consider moving some guys. ESPN’s Matt Bowen and Jeremy Fowler put out their Top 25 trade candidates by potential value, and included several Eagles.

At No. 8 on the list is CB Riq Woolen, who is considered a fit for teams like the Lions, Panthers, and Steelers.

“What Fowler is hearing: When I talk to rival teams about which players Philly might move, Woolen’s name comes up fairly often. He’s a high-upside corner and 2027 free agent whose $1.26 million base salary could help facilitate a trade (much of his $12 million in guarantees came via signing or restructured bonuses).

Predicted chance of getting traded: 35%“

Eagles guard Landon Dickerson sits at No. 12 on the list, with Fowler explaining that the relationship between Dickerson and the team doesn’t feel right — something we’ve covered, as well. The NFL insider also noted that the Eagles are in position to recoup some draft capital as they look to go younger up front. Still, they only put Dickerson’s chance of being traded around 25 percent.

Tight end Dallas Goedert and wide receiver Hollywood Brown were also honorable mentions on the list, which makes sense given that they’re playing on one-year contracts.

The Eagles were also listed among the list as a potential landing spot for Bengals EDGE Shemar Stewart, a trade that Fowler suggests would be for a third-rounder.

“What Bowen sees on tape: Stewart has played just eight snaps this season, so teams would be betting on potential with the 2025 first-rounder. Stewart is an explosive mover with the physical profile to play on the edge, but he has yet to develop a refined pass-rush plan. He has two career sacks.“

Coming off a Monday night game and with a short week, Howie Roseman and team’s front office might be taking their time to picture their overall approach to building this roster over the next few years. But the GM has some big decisions to make about the direction of the team this year, and moving forward.

item.title: What to know about the Chiefs signing Justin Tucker to the practice squad
item.description: Kansas City is bringing in a former All-Pro kicker to the practice squad.
item.content:encoded:
On Wednesday morning, we led “Arrowheadlines” with rumors that the Kansas City Chiefswould be bringing in competition for kicker Harrison Butker. Sam McDowell of The Kansas City Star followed up a few hours later with a more notable name than anyone expected: Justin Tucker, reportedly being signed to the practice squad today.

In his 13-year career with the Baltimore Ravens, Tucker is a five-time first-team All-Pro, seven-time Pro Bowler, and a member of the All-Decade team from the 2010s.

He also hasn’t played football since 2024, a primary factor being the 10-game suspension the NFL hit him with in the summer of 2025; the discipline stemmed from 16 accusations of “inappropriate sexual behavior” by massage therapists. Tucker has denied the allegations.

He had a rough final season in Baltimore, and the Ravens called cutting ties with their all-time placekicker a “football decision” at the time, but it’s hard to overlook the suspension-worthy allegations, which ranged from 2012-2016, according to McDowell’s report in The Star.

After a Pro Bowl campaign in 2023, a season that ended in an AFC Championship loss to the Chiefs, Tucker’s field-goal percentage dropped to 73% in 2024 with multiple missed point-after attempts for the first time in five years.

Earlier this season, he tried out for the Miami Dolphins, but the winless Dolphins (at the time) went with Zane Gonzalez instead. According to Jesse Newell of The Athletic, the Chiefs were the fifth team since his suspension to host him for a tryout.

In Kansas City, Tucker reportedly beat out former Missouri Tigers kicker Harrison Mevis — who was released by the Los Angeles Rams a few weeks ago — and Ben Sauls, according to Ian Rapoport of NFL Network.

The most memorable moment in Tucker’s career in relation to the Chiefs was the pre-game antics from the 2023 season’s AFC Championship. Quarterback Patrick Mahomes and tight end Travis Kelce kicked and threw equipment of Tucker’s away from where they were warming up on the field.

The move comes after Butker has struggled over the last two games, missing three field goals and a point-after attempt. We will hear from head coach Andy Reid at the podium around Noon Arrowhead time today and will likely get more information on whether the 36-year-old Tucker will fill in for an injured Butker or is just insurance for Kansas City’s all-time kicker moving forward.

item.title: Eagles News: Nick Foles says “there is dysfunction in Philly”
item.description: Philadelphia Eagles news and links for 10/28/26.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation!

Accurate or not, these are the kind of sentiments that will be expressed when a team is on a big losing streak. It is notable that Nick Foles, who usually seems pretty positive in his analysis, is more harsh here.

Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links …

Eagles legend calls Philly’s culture dysfunctional — Nick Sirianni responds: ‘That crap’ – NJ.com

“There is dysfunction in Philly,” Foles said on his podcast. “It was little things for me. It wasn’t the execution that got me. It was culture things. The number one thing isn’t scheme, a fancy coordinator, it’s culture. In Philadelphia, for the better of the past couple decades, they have had really good culture. Something is changing.” During the offseason, Foles feared that the Eagles would fall apart after they pushed a legendary coach out of the building. “When they got rid of [former Eagles offensive line coach] Jeff Stoutland, that really pissed me off,” Foles said. “I knew something bad was gonna happen. He is a great coach. For him not to get the respect that he deserves, that frustrates me. When guys are getting hit and offensive lineman are near them, is someone going to pick up the running back? He just got hit in the backfield. That culture with Jeff, that would never fly. When we got hit, we were picked up right away by the offensive line.“

Eagles-Cowboys Film Review: Most annoying defensive performance of the Vic Fangio era – BGN

I have made plenty of excuses for the Eagles’ defense this year. There have been games when I thought this unit fought hard and received very little help from the other side of the ball. There is absolutely no excuse for this one. Monday Night Football. At home against the Cowboys. Most of the defense’s best players were available, including the expensive “superstars” up front. And this was the performance? I can’t remember coming away from a game this annoyed about a defense since the Super Bowl LVII defeat vs. the Chiefs. The Cowboys scored on seven of nine possessions, rushed for 204 yards, and finished with 416 total yards at 6.4 yards per play. The Eagles recorded zero sacks, zero quarterback hits, and zero rushing tackles for loss. After the offense opened the second half with a 17-play touchdown drive that took 9:16 off the clock, the defense immediately surrendered another touchdown. We cannot blame the offense for that. This defense had a long rest and a lead, and still couldn’t get a stop.

NFL Week 8 latest intel, buzz questions, news, fantasy tips: What we’re hearing – ESPN

Fowler: Mystery surrounds the Eagles’ plans. It’s unclear at this point whether GM Howie Roseman conducts a fire sale. But some rival teams are expecting at least mild unloading. Perhaps the most interesting team is the Tampa Bay Bucs, who typically are not subtractors by nature. Normally, this would be a natural time for a roster mini-reset. But despite the 2-5 record, the Bucs are alive in the NFC South, which they’ve won four of the past five years. Win enough divisional games and the overall record doesn’t matter as much. I do believe, had the Bucs lost last week to fall to 1-6, they would be actively discussing dealing players. Graziano: We didn’t really address the Eagles in our trade-deadline portion of this column, but my sense is that things could go either way — or a little bit of both — for them ahead of the trade deadline. They have veterans on expiring contracts (cornerback Riq Woolen, receiver Hollywood Brown and tight end Dallas Goedert) who could be of interest to contending teams and help Philly out with draft-pick compensation. But the Eagles are loaded with picks already thanks to previous trades. They dealt their 2027 third-rounder for Jonathan Greenard but are projected to get a third-round compensatory pick due to the free agent loss of Jaelan Phillips. And they have extra first- and second-round picks in the 2028 draft due to the trades of A.J. Brown and Cam Jurgens. The Eagles aren’t desperate to refill their coffers. But they’ll always listen, in both directions. If they get a good enough offer for a player who isn’t part of their future plans, as was the case with Jurgens a couple of weeks ago, they’ll be open to it. And if they see a chance to add a player who might be more than a two-month rental, as the Texans did with Marvin Harrison Jr., they’ll be open to that as well.

Will the Eagles be sellers at the trade deadline? A look at Howie Roseman’s options – The Athletic

There have been trade deadlines when Roseman was not an aggressive buyer. He was also a strategic seller at times (such as trading veteran Isaac Sopoaga in 2013 when Bennie Logan was ready to take over at nose tackle). But no deadline has looked like this, with a losing record and attractive pending free agents available. That’s why the focus should be on players such as Ojomo, Woolen and Goedert. One factor to consider is whether the Eagles would prefer to keep Ojomo and Woolen and benefit from the compensatory formula. (Goedert, who is expected to be a post-June 1 cut because of a poison pill in his contract, would not qualify for a compensatory pick.) The Eagles have benefited from compensatory picks in recent years, though they also needed those pending free agents to contribute down the stretch. That might not be the case this December. Trading the player at the deadline rather than letting him leave in the offseason could mean the pick arrives as early as April’s draft, and it also lets the Eagles be aggressive in free agency if they choose. (Incoming free agents could cancel out outgoing free agents in the compensatory pick formula.)

Which Eagles players are untouchable at the trade deadline? – PhillyVoice

Nobody is trading for them in their current state. QB Jalen Hurts: Hurts of course has blood clots in his lungs, and his season is over. Depending on how things play out after this mess of a season is over, particularly in the case of a head coaching change, a trade of Hurts should be viewed as a possibility, but not until the offseason.

Selling – Iggles Blitz

The trade deadline isn’t until November 10th so it is interesting that the Colts made these moves so early. They set the market. That should lead to more calls between teams. The Niners and Seahawks just got better. That could cause the Bears, Lions, Rams, or other NFC contenders to feel forced to make a move. Buffalo needs help for their defense. The Chiefs need a WR. There should be plenty of activity. Nick Sirianni talked about the Eagles going 6-2 down the stretch in 2021 and how that helped the 2022 and 2024 teams make the Super Bowl. That’s why the Eagles will keep competing and doing everything they can to win. NFL players also have short careers. You don’t want to throw away a season. You don’t want apathy to set in. You don’t want to ruin good culture. We can debate if that has already started to go. I still think the Eagles have the right kind of guys in the building. We’ll find out more about that over the final 10 games. I mentioned players playing for their jobs. Sirianni will be coaching for his. We’ll find out just how much the players think of him with the way they play for the rest of the season.

What we learned from Eagles-Cowboys: Forget 2021 comparisons, Howie Roseman should sell at the trade deadline – PHLY Eagles

Going back through some of the media scrums I missed while attending Nick Sirianni’s news conference last night, this quote from Cooper DeJean about mentally handling the adversity the team is facing jumped out to me. “It’s been tough, to be honest,” DeJean said. “With the success that we’ve had the last couple years, it’s been tough to lose games, even lose snaps out there on defense. Not to look at the past, but we made a lot of plays the last couple years. There’s been plays that we’ve made that we haven’t made this season. You have to find a way to get past that, though, and learn from it. But I’d be lying if I said it’s easy to just move on from those plays. You get beat, you mess up a fit, whatever it is. It’s tough to move on from that. But that’s the mindset you have to have in this league.” DeJean is seemingly a player devoid of confidence all of a sudden. He gave up a touchdown catch to Lamb in the corner of the end zone Monday night and was at fault for at least one more completion and a few missed tackles. I wrote last week about the sudden leadership void we’re seeing with the Eagles in the wake of Jalen Hurts going on injured reserve and Lane Johnson retiring. Those absences compounded the offseason departures of veteran leaders like Nakobe Dean and Reed Blankenship and help explain how things have regressed so quickly for the Eagles defense. I’d argue that void has acutely affected DeJean as he tries navigating the most turbulent stretch of his professional career and perhaps his entire playing career overall.

Emotional Landon Dickerson pins blame on himself after loss – NBCSP

Landon Dickerson was emotional in the wake of the Eagles’ 38-21 loss to the Cowboys on Monday night at the Linc. It was a loss he pinned on himself. “It’s frustrating,” the left guard said. “I let my guys down. I didn’t play good enough. These guys work their a— off to come in here and compete every day. I just wasn’t good enough.” Dickerson, 28, returned to the lineup on Monday after missing the last five games on Injured Reserve with a bone bruise in his right knee. But he was moving better in this game than the last time we saw him and he did some good things. He just couldn’t stop thinking about a couple bad reps in the fourth quarter. “F—ing the two plays at the end, f—ing losing us the game,” Dickerson said.

Fantasy Football Red-Zone Report: NFL Week 8 – PFF

Edge offense. The Philadelphia Eagles rank sixth in red-zone conversion rate (53.8%) and 17th in RZ EPA per play (+0.057). This week’s opponent, the Commanders defense, ranks 31st in red-zone conversion rate allowed (60.7%) and 31st in RZ EPA allowed per play (+0.422).

Makai Lemon reflects on his first career touchdown – PhiladelphiaEagles.com

“Whatever the team asks me to do, just making sure I do that and (show) up every week,” Lemon said after the game. The first-round pick out of the University of Southern California has seen his role and production continue to grow over the course of the season. After recording 65 receiving yards through the first four games, Lemon ‘s production jumped with a 49-yard performance against Jacksonville in Week 5. Under the primetime lights, Lemon stepped up and produced his best game so far as an Eagle. The rookie caught seven out of eight targets for 67 yards and a touchdown – the first of his young NFL career. Lemon is the first Eagles rookie to have at least five receptions, 50 receiving yards and a receiving touchdown in a game since DeVonta Smith did so three times in his 2021 rookie season. Most importantly, he looked at ease in the offense. “The more that I progress throughout the season, I definitely feel like it’s getting more comfortable, more familiar with the game,” Lemon said. “The more you do something, the more you’re going to get comfortable at it. So, that’s where I’m at.”

Ravens sign G Michael Jordan after Vega Ioane injury – Baltimore Beatdown

[Former Eagles guard] Michael Jordan, 28, was originally a Bengals fourth-round pick in 2019. He started 19 games over his first two seasons – due in part to Cincinnati’s offensive line injuries – but was out of the game day picture entering 2021. Jordan was waived in September and later picked up by the Panthers, who badly needed O-line help and installed him as their starting left guard to close out the season. He served as a backup the following year before 11 starts for the Patriots in 2024 and nine for the Buccaneers last year, again as a result of his teammates’ injuries.

Cardinals work out four receivers, sign one – Revenge Of The Birds

The five players included QB Jack Plummer, and receivers Zay Jones, [former Eagles tryout] James Proche, Xavier Guillory, and Ronnie Bell. After the workout, Arizona inked Jones to a contract.

Broncos sign WR Eli Pancol to practice squad, release DB Ugo Amadi – Denver Gazette

The Broncos signed Eli Pancol to the practice squad. To make room, they released [former Eagles] veteran defensive back Ugo Amadi, whom they had signed Oct. 9.

NFL power rankings: Nick’s picks for how teams stack up before Week 8 – Big Blue View

No. 17 — New York Giants (4-2-1) | (20th) 📈 3 spots. The Giants just pulled off one of the biggest upsets of the year in Houston as 10.5-point underdogs on the road. The team responded to critical coaching and dominated both sides of the football. Still, overtime was necessary because of two missed kicks, among a few other things. Nevertheless, the Giants forced their fifth three-and-out in overtime and scored three plays later on a 30-yard touchdown run. The Giants are a different team under John Harbaugh.

Flawed Cowboys defense does enough versus Eagles – Blogging The Boys

Final grade: C. This Eagles offense is in absolute shambles at this point in time. They are down one franchise quarterback, two starting receivers, multiple offensive linemen, and too many running backs to count. This needed to be a game where the Dallas defense started fast and never looked back. They eventually got going, but it took too much time against a terrible Philadelphia offensive unit. The Eagles came out and punched the Cowboys defense in the mouth right from the start. The first drive took just four plays in just over two minutes to go 75 yards for a touchdown. A horrendous start that had us pulling out our hair (if you had any left).

How Commanders LB Sonny Styles removed all doubt with stellar start – Hogs Haven

Styles has played just six games to this point, but the evaluation’s pretty clear. This dude is legit. We officially learned that in Week 3, when he covered Seattle running back Jadarian Price like a blanket on a deep route, with the expertly knocked away with an outstretched arm. Price runs like a gazelle. Styles is 6-foot-5 and 245 pounds. Guys that big shouldn’t run like that. The play we recall here wasn’t the biggest stat. We’re talking about a pass defensed on a day where he had five tackles, a forced fumble and an interception.

The Vikings are undefeated, not historic – SB Nation

“Historic” has become one of those buzz words that gets far too overused when discussing players and/or teams. It’s right up there with “generational talent.” If every team is “historic” or if every good player is “generational,” then the word loses meaning, and really no one and nothing is worthy of those classifications. And yeah, I know this sounds like you’re reading another edition of Cranky Blowhard Quarterly, but the discourse around the Minnesota Vikings has become one that has led to a very good defensive unit being put in a class they don’t belong in, and a team that, while 6-0, is being heralded as a real contender when it shouldn’t be.

item.content:encoded:
According to NFL Network’s lead league insider Ian Rapoport, Denver Broncos star wide receiver Jaylen Waddle suffered an aggravation of his previous chest injury during Sunday’s victory over the Cardinals. Rapoport adds that Waddle’s availability this week will be based on how practice goes.

9NEWS Denver’s Mike Klis also adds that Waddle is expected to be listed as questionable for Sunday’s game vs. the Chiefs, but there is hope that he can play. Klis adds, “It’s the Chiefs after all.”

As we know, Waddle injured his shoulder on a late 4th-quarter reverse call where Waddle bobbled the ball and landed hard on his chest/shoulder when recovering the ball. After the play, Waddle was slow to get up and was in obvious pain. After the game, Broncos head coach Sean Payton called the play “dumb” and asked the media why they did not ask him about the play call.

“Why didn’t anybody ask me about the dumb reverse call? That would be one of the first calls. Alright, I’m
going to answer. Everyone ask the question. It was awful. I’m sorry. If you look it up — in 2008, in a
similar situation, even a more radical reverse, (former Saints RB Reggie Bush) fumbled (and) Tampa Bay
beat us. I know better. Every once in a while you fall in love with a play. That would have been a good
question.”

Thankfully. Waddle’s injury seems like a short-term thing, and there is hope that he can play vs. the Chiefs on Sunday. However, we need to pay attention to the injury report this week to determine his status. Klis notes that he will be questionable, but it seems like his availability will come down to pain tolerance. We don’t know the exact chest/shoulder injury he suffered, but he was limited for two practices before practicing fully on Friday. So, we will have to see if Waddle will be limited for today’s practice or not. A DNP to start the week would not be a great sign for his availability on Sunday.

This game vs. the Chiefs will be a big one. First, the Broncos will look to bounce back after their embarrassing Week 1 loss to the Chiefs to open the season. More importantly, if the Broncos were to win this game, they would move to the top of the AFC West. A loss would put them at 5-3, two games behind the Chiefs in the loss column, and they would have the tie-breaker due to the in-season sweep of the Broncos.

So, it’s a bit of a must-win game for the Broncos if they want to win the AFC West.

Hopefully, Waddle can go and play through this injury, but we will have to wait and see. The Broncos have their first practice of the week today and we will see whether or not is able to practice today. Stay tuned to Mile High Report for today’s injury report and any and all updates on Waddle’s status for this Sunday’s game vs. the Chiefs.
