item.title: A.J. Brown, Jalen Coker headline Week 8's Regression Files
item.description: A close look at offensive environments and which players are running hold and cold headed into Week 8
item.content:encoded:
Air yards, whether we like it or not — and most fantasy folks definitely do not like it — are a good measure of a pass catcher’s opportunity and the type of passing volume in a given offense. That air yards don’t always translate into real, edible receiving yards is just part of our frustrating little game. We make small bets here and there and hope things break right from week to week and prove our process correct more often than not. It’s not any more complicated than that, even if we desperately want it to be.

Over the past few seasons I have used this space to talk mostly about guys with exceptionally high or low touchdown rates. Air yards has mostly been a side issue in the Regression Files. That will change in 2026: I want Regression Files to be your weekly go-to for (freely available) air yards data and what it means for your various fantasy football teams.

Thanks to my friend and fellow football analytics nerd Brad Beatson, we have a more organized way of not only tracking air yards data, but a measure of which pass catchers are seeing accurate targets and which guys are not. The latter phenomenon is known in nerdy football circles as Prayer Yards, or inaccurate passes that technically award a bunch of air yards to a given receiver who rarely has a chance of converting those air yards into real yards as the football sails over their head or out of bounds or wherever else.

In this space I’m going to look powerfully into total team air yards trends, players seeing plentiful prayer yards, and those who are outperforming their air yards profile and (perhaps) due for the bad kind of regression.

Moves to Make Before Week 8 Fantasy Football: Buy Chris Olave, sell Ashton Jeanty
Chris Olave and A.J. Brown are fantasy football buy-low trade targets.
  • Alfredo Brown,

Total Team Air Yards

Below is a quick look at league leaders in total team air yards through seven weeks of the regular season, sorted by total air yards per game.

Green Bay Packers

Don’t worry too much about our reigning air yards kings of Wisconsin. The Packers in Week 7 against the pass-funnel Lions led the league with 438 team air yards, nearly 200 more than the tenth-place team on the week.

Matthew Golden had a league-leading 160 air yards against the Lions while Christian Watson finished with 88 air yards, the 17th most on the week. They both just ran cold. So it goes. Golden, by the bye, leads the NFL in air yards (941) and it’s not particularly close.

With Josh Jacobs back in the fold, the Packers did the right thing and kept flinging it. They were 6.5 percent over their expected pass rate and ranked fourth in neutral early-down pass rate. Shoutout Matt LaFleur for not being a total coward!

New York Giants

The G-people since Week 4 lead the NFL with an utterly ridiculous 418 total air yards per game. This — as you know if you roster Giants players — has changed the entire composition of the New York offense and injected never-ending life into Malik Nabers.

In Week 7 against the pass-funnel Texans defense, JJ McCarthy and the Giants went ultra-run-heavy (9 percent below their expected pass rate) and still piled up 318 total air yards, the sixth most of the week. That’s what happens when your QB has an average depth of target of nearly 9 yards, as McCarthy did against Houston. That, I think, should continue next week when the Giants take on an Eagles defense allowing the tenth most total team air yards per game.

LA Rams

With Davante Adams done for the year, it looks like Sean McVay is ready and willing to go all-in on the three tight end thing. The Rams in Week 7 against the Raiders had three tight ends on the field for more than 70 percent of their plays. Davis Allen was the lucky one with two touchdown grabs on just 12 routes.

LA was 2.2 percent below its expected pass rate against the Raiders. It was their run-heaviest game since the Week 1 Australia nightmare. The Rams weren’t entirely run-obsessed though: Only six teams had a higher neutral early-down pass rate in Week 7.

As for the air yards: The Rams posted 206 total team air yards against Vegas, the seventh fewest of any team in the league in Week 7. That pales in comparison to the 403 team air yards they averaged from Week 2 — following the Australia nightmare — to Week 6, when they lost Adams to the worst hamstring injury anyone has ever seen. Puka Nacua will continue to get there every week no matter what. Guessing which of the three Rams tight ends will get there threatens to drive the entire fantasy football industry insane.

Washington Commanders

Here's what I wrote last week about the post-McLaurin Commanders offense and who should benefit from all the vacated targets and air yards in the coming weeks.

Arizona Cardinals

The Cards are finally looking like the Cards we know from 2025, the ones who blessed us every week with 2.6 million air yards, the Cards who showered us with fraudulent garbage time production the way Kirk Cousins has in Vegas this season.

Over the past month the Cardinals have averaged 339 total air yards per game, the seventh most in the NFL. In Week 7 they were second only to the Packers in total air yards, with the tenth-highest pass rate over expected.

Sadly for Michael Wilson drafters, it was Jalen Brooks who accounted for a team-leading 119 air yards (33 percent) while Trey McBride had 98 air yards. Wilson was left with scraps: 86 air yards while being targeted on a somewhat concerning 16 percent of his pass routes.

The Cardinals haven't been able to get Michael Wilson many easy opportunities since the Marv trade, but he's still been making some impressive plays: pic.twitter.com/FvnBeDPSTQ

— Theo Mackie (@theo_mackie) October 27, 2026

Now for your weekly dose of cold comfort: Wilson ranks ninth among all receivers in air yards since Week 4. He’s only converted 40 percent of those air yards into real yards, down from 46 percent over the season’s first few games. The problem is Jacoby Brissett’s shocking inaccuracy on long balls. Brissett on the season has completed five of his 26 throws of more than 20 yards; he’s 22 percent below his expected completion rate on those attempts. He ranks 36th out of 40 qualifying quarterbacks in EPA per pass on deep throws.

Brissett has never been a superb downfield passer, but it has never been this bad. Perhaps with a little improvement from Jacoby, Wilson can start turning his air yards into edible receiving yards for your hungry fantasy squad. Arizona averaging nearly 70 offensive snaps per game over the past four weeks should help everyone in this miserable offense.

Here are teams averaging the fewest total team air yards per game.

Minnesota Vikings

There’s nothing doing with the Vikings offense. The whole operation stinks. Obviously they’d be much better with JJ McCarthy at the helm but the kid was far too annoying to keep around any longer. I get that.

Kyler “Mid” Murray and the Minnesota offense in Week 7 had 201 total air yards against the Colts (while operating 4.4 percent below their expected pass rate). It’s only the third time this season they’ve cleared the 200 air yards mark. That’s bleak.

This means even when Justin Jefferson dominates air yards — on Sunday he accounted for 31 percent of the Vikings’ air yards — it doesn’t amount to much. Elic Ayomanor and Mason Taylor had more than Jefferson’s 62 air yards on Sunday. Jordan Addison, who ranks 58th in air yards this season, is all but unplayable in 12-team leagues thanks to this hideous offensive environment.

You’re just hoping and praying for touchdowns if you’re starting Minnesota pass catchers for now. Sorry to get religious.

New York Jets

It feels a little odd to write this as Omar Cooper, Jr. goes ballistic every week: The Jets offense is an air yards graveyard that probably can’t support more than one pass catcher per week, if that.

Even as Geno Smith went for 287 yards and three touchdowns against Miami in Week 7, the Jets offense produced a meager 205 total team air yards, the fifth fewest of the week. The Jets since Week 4 are averaging 200 total air yards per game; only the Bucs have a lower mark.

Geno zipped this one into Omar Cooper Jr. for a 60-yard gain

MIAvsNYJ on CBS/Paramount+
Stream on @NFLPluspic.twitter.com/EeuCoD4kwN

— NFL (@NFL) October 25, 2026

The whole thing destroys the case for Adonai Mitchell as a high-upside WR3/4 option. Mitchell, in his return to the lineup in Week 7, saw 18 air yards while running 51 percent of the team’s routes. Mason Taylor, meanwhile, led the Jets with 73 air yards, a gaudy 43 percent share.

Increased involvement from Cooper — who leads the team in air yards and has been targeted on 24 percent of his pass routes over the past two games — along with Taylor and Mitchell could make things awfully dicey for Garrett Wilson over the next couple months. Wilson over the past couple weeks has seen 21 percent of the Jets’ air yards and 15 percent of the team’s targets. From Week 1-4, Wilson enjoyed a 29 percent target share and a 48 percent air yards share.

New York’s offense operates at the NFL’s fifth-slowest pace and only the Broncos, Dolphins, and Titans average fewer offensive plays per game. It is an undeniably ugly fantasy environment right now.

Tennessee Titans

The Titans are trying that thing where you run your offense at a faster pace and produce more plays and dropbacks and yes, air yards. In Week 7 against the Browns the Titans produced 281 total air yards, the 11th most in the NFL. Headed into Week 7 they had averaged 225 team air yards per game.

It’s not a big change, but perhaps enough to make Carnell Tate more reliable as a high-variance WR3. The aforementioned Ayomanor got more involved in Week 7, leading the Titans with 71 air yards and turning that opportunity into three receptions for 44 yards. It’s a situation worth monitoring if the Titans stick with it. Only four teams have a higher offensive pace on the season.

Prayer Yards Warriors (Players who could see positive regression)

AJ Brown (NE)

Prayer yards rate: 74 percent

Brown’s listed prayer yards rate does not include his Week 1 outing, which was cut short by one of the highest ankle sprains in recorded medical history. As AJB drafters know all too well, Brown has run colder than cold (ice cold) over the past couple weeks. Someone should lend him some sugar; he is your neighbor.

Anyway, Brown has accounted for 46 percent of New England’s air yards over the past two games (and 23.5 percent of the team’s targets). It’s a gaudy number that should mean AJB can produce actual yards and maybe even touchdowns if/when he stops playing terribly. His role in the Patriots offense — which ranks seventh in pass rate over expected since Week 4 — means he needs to remain in all lineups ahead of the team’s Week 8 matchup against the regularly-wrecked Miami secondary.

A mere 11 receivers have a higher expected fantasy points per game than AJB since Week 6. His actual points per game? Forty-second among wideouts.

Jalen Coker (CAR)

Prayer yards rate: 76 percent

Coker has run pretty dang cold over the Panthers’ past four games. His prayer yards rate over that span is the fifth-highest among wideouts who have seen at least ten targets. Like I said: Cold.

Probably you weren’t going to bench Coker ahead of Carolina’s Thursday night game against the Packers. But if you were tinkering with the idea of finding a Coker replacement, close your eyes and trust that the Regression Reaper will make a Week 8 visit to the Panthers WR1. Coker on the season ranks 18th among receivers in expected PPR points per game, just behind Zay Flowers and Parker Washington. He’ll be OK.

Bryce Lance (NO)

Prayer yards rate: 90 percent

Lance, who didn’t do a whole lot in Week 7 after sneaking his way into the Regression Files, lands here once again because nine in ten air yards coming his way have gone incomplete. That’s a hideous and likely-unsustainable rate that could correct itself. He remains a desperation flex option for those in 28-team leagues.

Harold Fannin, Jr. (CLE)

Prayer yards rate: 66 percent

Two-thirds of Fannin’s air yards over the past four weeks have been for naught in a Cleveland offense that’s usually on the pass-first side of things. Pat Freiermuth is the only tight end in the league with a season-long higher prayer yards rate than Fannin. Fannin’s (positive) regression seems to have begun in Week 7 against the Titans when he caught six of nine targets for 91 yards.

That good kind of regression could continue in Week 8 against a Steelers defense giving up nearly 300 total team air yards per game this year.

Bullseye Enjoyers (Players who could see negative regression)

Jaylin Noel (HOU)

Bullseye rate: 100 percent

Noel lands here again because, well, all 180 of his air yards over the past five weeks have been completed. Accordingly, Noel is well above his expected fantasy points per game over that stretch.

The return of Tank Dell and the (playing time) emergence of Marvin Harrison, Jr. led to a 52 percent route participation rate for Noel in Week 7. The negative regression will continue until morale improves.

Caleb Douglas (MIA)

Bullseye rate: 60 percent

It’s not that Douglas’ bullseye rate is particularly egregious. It’s what he’s done after the catch that is — per the Regression Reaper — totally unsustainable. Last week’s box score explosion against the Jets saw Douglas score 21 fantasy points. His expected fantasy output: 8.3 points, or 54th among wideouts on the week.

Caleb Douglas took this one all the way.

MIAvsNYJ on CBS/Paramount+
Stream on @NFLPluspic.twitter.com/hb8mEQrB80

— NFL (@NFL) October 25, 2026

Miami’s offense has (smartly) gone ultra-turbo-giga run heavy over the team’s past couple games. Against the Jets they were nearly 10 percent below their expected pass rate. That leaves Douglas and the rest of the Dolphins wideouts unlikely to see the sort of target and air yards volume to be reliable in any fantasy format. The Dolphins since Week 5 rank 25th in total team air yards per game.

Omar Cooper, Jr. (NYJ)

Bullseye rate: 95 percent

Pointing out potential negative regression for fun players like Cooper is part of the job, I suppose. I’m a Cooper fan and take no pleasure in saying there’s (almost) no way he can keep doing what he’s doing in the Jets offense.

A mere eight of Cooper’s 160 air yards over the past two games have gone unconverted. He’s averaging about seven fantasy points per game over expected. The good news is that Cooper’s expected fantasy points since Week 6 ranks among the top-20 receivers. Even a little bad regression should keep Cooper in 12-team league starting lineups. Fun is still legal for now.

Good Air Yards Matchups: Week 8

Browns at Steelers

CLE air yards allowed per game: 353 (4th)
CLE neutral pass rate against: 56 percent (12th)
CLE pass rate over expected against: -0.1 percent (19th)

There aren't a whole lot of options for those of us looking for air yards-rich environments in Week 8. This Browns-Steelers matchup qualifies as one because Cleveland allows the fourth most total air yards per game and the Steelers allow the 14th most. We work with what we have.

The Steelers have seen the league's fifth highest pass rate over expected against them this year, and only Detroit opponents have a higher neutral pass rate than Steelers opponents. It should make a lot of pass catchers interesting here, including Denzel Boston, KC Concepcion, the aforementioned Fannin, DK Metcalf, the Steelers tight ends, and of course, Germie Bernard.

Falcons vs. Bucs

ATL air yards allowed per game: 356 (3rd)
ATL neutral pass rate against: 58 percent (7th)
ATL pass rate over expected against: +6 percent (3rd)

I think we can safely throw out the Bucs' Week 7 massacre of the Panthers in which Tampa was 30 percent below its expected pass rate and totaled a miserable 67 team air yards. This week they face off against an extreme pass funnel in the Falcons, a defense that has seen six of their seven opponents exceed their expected pass rate.

Maybe, just maybe, that can put Chris Godwin and Tampa pass catchers in play as viable 12-team options this week. The Bucs defense, meanwhile, profiles as a top-10 pass funnel on the season. That could fuel volume for Drake London and Kyle Pitts here.

item.title: At least Ashton Jeanty is helping as receiver
item.description: How did 2025 draft class fare?
item.content:encoded:
Here is a look at how the Las Vegas Raiders’ 2025 draft class fared ina 35-21 home loss to the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday and what to look for Sunday at the New York Jets.

Ashton Jeanty:

The No. 6 overall draft pick played 72 percent of the snaps, a week after playing 58 percent. Jeanty struggled as a rusher again as he had just 15 yards on eight carries. He has averaged less than three yards a carry in five games this season. He did have a season high eight catches for 61 yards. He is tied for the league high among running backs.

Jack Bech:

The second-round pick is on the injured reserve with a fractured forearm. His practice window is expected to open this week.

Darien Porter:

The third-round pick played 59 percent of the defensive snaps, his least amount since regaining his starting job three weeks ago. It will be interesting to see how much he plays against the Jets.

Caleb Rogers:

The third-round pick took over for the benched Jackson Powers-Johnson for the second straight week. He did struggle in the running game and will likely have to earn his starting job on a weekly basis.

Charles Grant:

The offensive lineman, taken in the third round, didn’t play on offense as usual, but he did log four snaps on special teams.

Dont’e Thornton:

The wide receiver, taken in the fourth round, was activated from the injured reserve and he will be ready to make his season debut Sunday.

Tonka Hemingway:

The fourth-round pick returned from a concussion he suffered in Week 5. He started and had a sack. But he didn’t have a great overall game.

JJ Pegues:

The defensive tackle, taken in the sixth round, was active for the third time this season. He played 16 snaps on defense and forced a fumble. It should get him another chance to play this week, especially with Jonah Laulu being released Tuesday.

Cody Lindenberg:

The seventh-round pick played three snaps at linebacker. It was his first defensive action of his career. He also played 16 snaps on special teams, which is his norm.

item.title: NFL betting, odds: 5 futures bets I'd make right now, including Jaxon Smith-Njigba to win MVP
item.description: Our NFL handicapper reveals five futures bets he likes. Can JSN actually win MVP?
item.content:encoded:
Futures bets are just that — a forward, future-looking index. 

We could easily tell you who should win the MVP after Week 7 (Brock Purdy), or Defensive Rookie of the Year (David Bailey), but last year at this time, Baker Mayfield MVP buzz was still crackling, and no one had Carson Schwesinger on their radar. 

Also, we’ve done some good work, grabbing players at better odds than they’re at now for those respective awards, gaining modest equity on Joe Burrow (from +850 to +500) at THE WINDOW, and Jacob Rodriguez (from +1500 to +600) in our preseason looks at the NFL award markets.

Then there’s a handful of players that we’ve missed the boat on, as +650 for Josh Allen feels like a steal now that he’s +160 for MVP, and Kenneth Walker has gone from 35-1 to +350 for Offensive Player of the Year.

With 10+ games to go, though, and the slow creep of recency bias that will be in voters minds still to come, we’ve got five futures bets worth adding, now that we’ve:

  1. Seen these teams play for almost two months

  2. Can see a path to improvement over the next two

Before we get on the back side of the mountain and momentum for various award candidates becomes an irresistible force, here are best value bets out there.

MVP: Jaxon Smith-Njigba (75-1)

As a bettor, it’s our job to predict what voters are going to do, not what we think they should do, fully aware this has turned into a quarterback award. If Saquon Barkley couldn’t wrestle it away from Josh Allen two years ago, it seems almost impossible for a non-QB to be the MVP. 

But what if that only applies to running backs? 

Enter Smith-Njigba, whose share of the offensive production on the Seahawks is comically high with a 50.2% receiving yardage share, a target share of almost 38% and eight of Seattle’s 18 touchdowns.

Last season, JSN was arguably the best receiver in the game because his stats were in lock-step with Puka Nacua. This season, he’s already 200+ yards and two touchdowns clear of any other receiver. Smith-Njigba edged out Nacua for the Offensive Player of the Year award, and while he could go back-to-back, at this rate, you could say he deserves something of a promotion this season to Most Valuable Player, given his quarterback leads the NFL in interceptions and Seattle’s Super Bowl MVP running back is now in Kansas City. 

In 2021, Cooper Kupp couldn’t win the first receiver MVP with almost 2,000 yards and 16 touchdowns, losing to Aaron Rodgers (and later winning Super Bowl MVP), but JSN is on pace for 2,100 yards and 19 touchdowns — if he finishes with numbers anywhere near that, he could get it done this season. 

There needs to be buzz for MVP, and, in his weekly appearance on the Ryen Russillo Podcast, Yahoo! Sports’ Nate Tice discussed this possibility, breaking the ice on a national conversation about JSN’s candidacy.

There’s a case to be made that the two favorites — Josh Allen and Brock Purdy — are going to be challenged to keep their winning up due to defense and injuries, respectively. The Seahawks seem primed to go on a heater. If they can track down the 49ers to nab the NFC West (+345), Smith-Njigba might steal the MVP as well. 

Offensive Player of the Year: Bijan Robinson (7-1)

Maybe Smith-Njigba has to settle for a second Offensive Player of the Year award, but if he wins MVP, or the season goes sideways for him, OPOY likely becomes a three-horse race between tailbacks. 

Kenneth Walker has the early lead for the rushing title, moving him up the odds board for OPOY. Jahmyr Gibbs was the preseason favorite, and hasn’t disappointed, but Bijan Robinson had to play two of seven games with Cooper Rush as his quarterback. 

Robinson’s numbers were actually pretty good with Rush at the helm, but since Michael Penix Jr. made his season debut, the Falcons’ offense has functioned well across the board. Plus, Atlanta’s defense has been surprisingly stout, helping the Falcons’ chances for more run-first situations in their final 10 games, and enough wins for voters to want to honor the team’s best player. 

Mix in the eye test, of Robinson being really fun to watch — already with seven long runs (tied with Walker for the league lead) — and some room for statistical improvement as a receiver, and you have a player ready to win Offensive Player of the Year.

Offensive Rookie of the Year: Omar Cooper Jr. (10-1)

Speaking of late-season stat runs, the second half of a season might be all that matters for Offensive Rookie of the Year. 

Early on, most rookies are still trying to stay healthy and find their way in a new team’s offense, and preseason OROY favorites Jeremiah Love and Jadarian Price have already missed time, while a handful of receivers on bad teams have performed …fine. 

  • Carnell Tate: 413 yards, 1 TD

  • Denzel Boston: 372 yards, 3 TD

  • KC Concepcion: 315 yards, 0 TD

Last season, Emeka Egbuka was more than just “fine,” racking up 677 receiving yards and six touchdowns in the first nine weeks, and was the clear-cut favorite for OROY.

Things turned in the latter half of the season, when Bryce Young and Tetairoa McMillan finally got on the same page. In the final 10 games of the 2025 season, T-Mac had 601 yards and five touchdowns, getting to 1,000 yards on the year, while Egbuka ran out of gas.

This season, Omar Cooper Jr. missed all but seven snaps of the Jets’ first five games, but since getting back on the field, he’s raccked up 11 catches for 218 yards and two touchdowns. It’s a small sample size, but it’s a nice start in trying to track down the receivers above him on the oddsboard.

If Cooper gets anywhere near 1,000 yards in just 12 full games, in a year where there’s no standout tailback or rookie starting QB, the voters will be all in, and he’s going to win Rookie of the Year. 

Comeback player of the year: Fred Warner (10-1)

We’ve got talking heads making a case for Deshaun Watson as Comeback Player of the Year — a thing that’s definitely not happening as long as human beings are still voting on these things. Meanwhile, Patrick Mahomes is still the odds-on favorite, even as he’s becoming less important to his own team’s offensive success. 

Neither player is currently a legitimate candidate for another NFL award, while Fred Warner has spent the early part of the season climbing the oddsboard for Defensive Player of the Year. However, it’s more probable that a pass-rusher will take that award, and Warner will just miss out. 

Warner’s well-liked, his visually-jarring dislocated ankle injury last season is something worthy to recognize a come-back from, and he has an interesting rehab story (already featured on ESPN’s Monday Night Countdown) about learning to swim at San Jose State. 

Given the type of injury, the physically-taxing nature of middle linebacker, and the level Warner’s performing at, he’s got the perfect resume for CPOY, once voters get past Mahomes’ merely decent play after a standard knee injury.

Best regular season record: Cincinnati Bengals (11-1)

He’s not exactly the Hulk, but the NFL is not going to like Joe Burrow when he’s very upset. The Ravens sure didn’t last week, after Burrow’s halftime locker room rant kick-started a dominant performance in the second half.

The 4-2 Bengals have already played at Baltimore (won) and Pittsburgh, and of their remaining 11 games, only a home game against the Chiefs has the chance of Cincinnati being even the smallest of underdogs. 

Until the second half in Baltimore on Sunday, Cincinnati’s offense hadn’t lit up the league in a nationally attention-grabbing way, but we know it’s more than capable. 

Defensively, we spent the entire offseason asking the Bengals to have merely an average unit to support the capabilities of the offense, and Cincinnati is on the edge of the top-10 in both EPA/Play and Success Rate on standard downs and game situations, as both new additions of Dexter Lawrence and Boye Mafe are rated in the top five at their position by PFF. 

A 13-4 record is a reasonable expectation, while the teams ahead of them have a tougher remaining schedule that could bring them down to that record or below.

You can find more valuable betting analysis from Yahoo Sports betting contributor, Matt Russell, at THE WINDOW.

item.title: Seahawks All-22 film review: The good and bad from a big Seahawks win over the Chiefs
item.description: The Seahawks dominated Mahomes and the Chiefs, but red-zone failures and Darnold’s mistakes show there’s still work to do.
item.content:encoded:
The Seattle Seahawks 20–3 win over the Kansas City Chiefs was fantastic. As I pointed out in the preview, a loss could have put the Seahawks in a difficult position, while a win would restore some confidence and put Seattle back in the mix.

Winning the division is still a long way off, but this result shows that there is enough talent on the field and on the coaching staff to make the necessary adjustments. After losses to the Washington Commanders and Denver Broncos, beating a quality opponent was essential. You can’t just rack up wins against weaker teams and then struggle when the level of competition goes up.

Of course, we have to account for the Chiefs’ injuries, especially along the offensive line. Seattle had its own injury issues, though, and that shouldn’t take away from a defense that held Patrick Mahomes and company to just three points.

The offense still showed some glaring issues, but there were also signs of improvement. The offensive line played a more solid game, the rushing attack grew as the game went on, and the defense showed it can compete against elite opponents.

This win doesn’t solve every problem, but it gives the Seahawks something they desperately needed: confidence and an opportunity to build some momentum.

The Good

1. The Seahawks defense was dominant

It’s hard to imagine a much better defensive performance than this one. The Seahawks held the Chiefs to just 3 points, 213 total yards, and 11 first downs, without allowing a single trip into the red zone. The three points tied the lowest total in any game started by Patrick Mahomes, while the 213 yards, 11 first downs, and zero red-zone trips were all new lows for the quarterback across his 153 career starts.

Seattle also outgained Kansas City by 197 yards. Across Mahomes’ 153 starts, only one game had featured a larger yardage differential against his team: the AFC Championship Game against the Patriots during the 2018 season. That puts Seattle’s dominance into perspective.

And this wasn’t simply a bad night for Kansas City; it was a normal night for the Seahawks defense. According to ESPN Research, Seattle became the first team since the 1984 Cleveland Browns to hold each of its first seven opponents of the season under 180 passing yards. The defense was also allowing just 3.99 yards per play, the lowest mark in the league and the fewest by any team through seven games since the 2019 New England Patriots.

The Seahawks’ performance against explosive plays reinforces that impression. They had allowed just 26 explosive plays through their first seven games — defined as runs of at least 12 yards or passes of at least 16 yards. According to TruMedia, that’s tied with the 2007 Indianapolis Colts for the fewest explosive plays allowed by any team through its first seven games since 2000.

All of this becomes even more impressive when you consider the opponent. Mahomes is one of the best quarterbacks in the NFL, Andy Reid remains one of the league’s top offensive minds, and Kenneth Walker III is capable of turning an ordinary play into a big gain. Seattle still contained the ground game and suffocated the opposing offense. Walker finished with just 36 rushing yards on 14 carries.

Kenneth Walker III entered the matchup averaging 133 rushing yards per game, leading the NFL in rushing production. Against his former team, however, he was held to just 36 yards on 14 carries, averaging 2.6 yards per attempt.

The Seahawks consistently set the edge and played sound team defense against the run. There were a few missed angles, but because the defense rallied to the ball as a unit, it was still able to make the play. On the rep above, Leonard Williams forces the running back inside, and Tyrice Knight makes the tackle for loss. The defensive tackle is the one who creates the play.

Another game in which Byron Murphy was unstoppable as a stand-up pass rusher. Great angle and plenty of explosiveness off the snap.

2. Nick Emmanwori showed his potential

Nick Emmanwori deserves a section of his own. Despite entering the game questionable, he played 100% of the defensive snaps and has shown unusual versatility for such a young player. He has played at least 50 snaps in each of the last four games.

His usage helps explain the potential Seattle has in this player. This season, Emmanwori has lined up approximately 36% of the time in the slot, 34% as a linebacker, and 27% near the line of scrimmage as an EDGE. His ability to play so many different roles allows the defense to change its looks without necessarily substituting personnel.

It took me a while to realize that Nick Emmanwori was the one making the tackle. He’s lined up on the opposite end of the line, and he isn’t just acting as a backside defender. He explodes off the snap and tracks down the ball carrier on the other side of the formation.

Here, he’s playing as an EDGE. Even though Travis Kelce, who isn’t exactly an elite blocker, has him engaged, Nick sheds the block after initially biting on Walker’s inside cut and still makes the tackle.

Now he’s impacting the game from the slot, covering a receiver downfield. When he’s asked to defend a vertical route without a double move or a change of direction, he can win the rep as if he were prime Richard Sherman.

Here, he shows outstanding instincts. He’s responsible for a zone with a tight end in his area, but he recognizes that the play is developing toward another receiver. He tries to help by closing the space and ends up getting a hand on the pass. Incredible. It’s just as impactful as that sensational pass breakup against the Texans last year.

This is pure athleticism. He reads the flow of the play, realizes Mahomes still has the ball, and takes off after the quarterback. No. 15 tries to work his magic, but under pressure, he ends up throwing an interception. Nick deserves a share of the credit for that turnover.

3. Jaxon Smith-Njigba continues to be the engine of the offense

Jaxon Smith-Njigba is putting together an extraordinary season and once again proved that he’s the engine of the Seahawks’ offense. Against Kansas City, he finished with 9 receptions for 150 yards and a touchdown. His impact was especially impressive in the first half, when he recorded six catches for 129 yards and a touchdown.

According to ESPN Research, those 129 receiving yards were the most JSN has recorded in any half of his NFL career. It was also the most receiving yards in a first half by a Seahawks player since Tyler Lockett recorded 133 yards on the road against the Arizona Cardinals in 2020.

His performance is part of a historic start to the season. JSN became the sixth player in NFL history to record at least 100 receiving yards in six of his team’s first seven games. He also became the fourth player in NFL history to reach at least 55 receptions and 800 receiving yards through his team’s first seven games.

He also passed Darrell Jackson to reach 28 receiving touchdowns in his first four seasons, the fifth-most in franchise history over that span.

I’ve seen people saying the Chiefs shouldn’t have put a rookie in Mansoor Delane on JSN. He played tight coverage against JSN on several occasions, including on the touchdown. Here, though, JSN absolutely burns the defensive back. The rookie tries to challenge him in press coverage, which isn’t a great idea against JSN. The safety providing over-the-top help takes a terrible angle, and JSN makes Kansas City pay with yards after the catch.

4. Signs of life from the offensive line and rushing attack

Emanuel Wilson finished the game with 24 carries for 100 yards and a touchdown, averaging 4.2 yards per attempt.

What’s most interesting is how his production was distributed. He had just 22 rushing yards in the first half but finished with 78 in the second. Over Seattle’s final three offensive drives, Wilson recorded 54 rushing yards, including the 21-yard touchdown run.

Wilson isn’t an explosive running back, and his limitations in burst and big-play ability remain evident. But when he’s used according to his strengths — running vertically and attacking the available gaps — he can be effective.

Zach Charbonnet should be able to help when he returns, but we shouldn’t expect his return to solve every problem with the rushing attack. What the Seahawks need is consistency. Against the Chiefs, Wilson and the offensive line showed signs that it is achievable.

Nick Kallerup makes this touchdown happen. He helps Eric Saubert with the initial block, then comes back to create the gap against No. 21. Wilson isn’t naturally a one-cut runner, but he recognizes the opening and gets into the end zone with barely anyone touching him.

Turning to the offensive line: after allowing 10 sacks over the previous two games, Seattle’s offensive line didn’t give up a single sack against Kansas City. That’s a significant improvement, both for Darnold’s performance and for the offense’s ability to sustain drives.

It doesn’t look as though Seattle made a major schematic overhaul. The difference against the Chiefs seems to have come primarily from better execution. The blocks were more consistent, Darnold had a better environment in which to operate, and the rushing attack produced without needing to rely on a big run every time.

5. The offense showed it can convert in difficult third-down situations

Despite the issues that still need to be addressed, there was a good reason to feel optimistic about the offense: Seattle converted 5-of-6 third-down attempts with at least nine yards to go. That’s the best conversion rate in a game with at least five such attempts since the Indianapolis Colts went 5-for-5 against the Houston Texans in Week 11 of 2008.

That deserves credit. It’s true that many of those long-yardage situations were also the result of problems earlier in the drive — inefficient play calls, short gains, and situations in which the offense put itself behind the chains. But converting five of six third-and-long attempts requires execution, and the Seahawks delivered.

AJ Barner also contributed with four catches for 42 yards. The offense showed it has the tools to move the ball even when the situation isn’t ideal. The next step is to make drives more consistent from the early downs and find more efficient ways to turn those advances into touchdowns.

Having Barner back opens up other dimensions of the offense, and he could be particularly useful in the red zone. Here, the play is designed to create space for him against man coverage. Shaheed’s route clears space on the lateral break, allowing Barner to make the catch and pick up his usual yards after the catch.

The Bad

1. Brian Fleury needs to fix the red-zone offense

Seattle had three red-zone possessions against Kansas City and came away with just six points: two field goals and one Sam Darnold interception. Those were two clear opportunities to score touchdowns that went to waste.

On the first trip, Seattle reached the Chiefs’ 9-yard line. Emanuel Wilson gained three yards, followed by a shovel pass to AJ Barner that lost a yard and nearly resulted in a fumble. Keep it simple until the offense can execute consistently.

Darnold then failed to complete the next attempt to Jaxon Smith-Njigba, and Jason Myers came on to kick a 25-yard field goal. The route concepts are so poor that there are essentially three players occupying two defenders at the top of the screen, Shaheed running an ineffective route at the bottom, and everyone else clustered around JSN. That makes the defense’s job easy.

What’s bizarre is that Fleury does a good job creating traffic and protecting releases in other situations. That’s something he should be calling much more often in the red zone. There’s no magic involved, but Shaheed’s route creates space for Kupp to read the opening and make a good catch.

The second opportunity was even more frustrating. After a 28-yard pass to JSN, Seattle reached the 2-yard line. George Holani lost a yard, and on the next play, Darnold threw an interception in the end zone. It was a huge opportunity to extend the lead before halftime, but the offense came away with nothing.

In the third quarter, the same story played out again. Seattle reached the 6-yard line, but a run by Velus Jones Jr. lost six yards. Fleury keeps calling these runs — at least this time it wasn’t Wilson — and Grey Zabel loses a key block at the second level. Charles Cross also gets beaten, leaving the running back with no chance.

Then came a delay-of-game penalty, which pushed the offense further back, and the next pass to Holani fell incomplete. Another field goal, this time from 35 yards. Of the 21 potential points available across those three opportunities, Seattle scored just six. No offense is going to be perfect in the red zone, but the problem for the Seahawks is how they keep wasting favorable opportunities.

Against Kansas City, the defense was dominant enough to make sure those failures didn’t cost Seattle the game. Against more efficient opponents, those wasted possessions could have much bigger consequences.

2. Sam Darnold still can’t put together a clean game

Sam Darnold had some positive moments against Kansas City, but he made another mistake that could have completely changed the game. The biggest concern isn’t just the interception; it’s the feeling that he isn’t learning from his mistakes.

After the loss to Denver, Darnold acknowledged that he’d been too greedy with his passes. Against Kansas City, he took another unnecessary risk in a situation where Seattle was already in position to score.

The problem is that Darnold looks like an all-or-nothing quarterback. At times, he finds a tight window, makes an excellent read, and delivers an accurate pass. At other times, he makes a disastrous decision that undoes all the work that came before it. There seems to be no middle ground.

The win doesn’t erase that concern. Darnold needs to show he can protect the ball, recognize when a play isn’t there, and accept that an incompletion can be better than trying to do everything himself.

On the interception, JSN’s and Shaheed’s routes again head in the same direction. Darnold has JSN open at one point, but he hesitates and is late with the throw. He ends up getting intercepted because the spacing of the routes has carried Shaheed’s defender into the passing lane.

Here, he leaves a big gain and a potential touchdown on the field. It’s another play designed to create space for Barner. The vertical routes have pushed the defenders deep into the end zone, which should leave Barner with plenty of room to run. But Darnold chooses to fire the ball in rather than put some air under it and clear the defender. He misses a huge opportunity.

Another missed opportunity. The concept is poor, and Darnold manages to buy time because the pressure arrives with just TWO rushers after Lucas loses his block. Holani and Darnold aren’t on the same page, and they miss out on a touchdown.

As mentioned, he played well overall, getting the ball out quicker and throwing with more confidence. But there’s still plenty of room for improvement. Here, he manages to escape what looked like a sure sack, albeit in somewhat awkward fashion, and runs for an important first down.

3. The defense still has room to improve

We’re looking at the negatives here, but this is actually a reason for optimism. The team put together a dominant performance, and it clearly hasn’t reached its ceiling yet. The Chiefs didn’t have much at wide receiver, yet they still found some production through their tight ends by exploiting the space behind the linebackers — an area opponents have been targeting at times this season.

Jones and Knight were caught out of position in coverage on a few occasions, even though both were dominant against the run. Here, there are communication issues and the defense isn’t properly set. Mahomes buys time because he isn’t contained in the pocket, and Jones abandons Kelce even though Knight is in position to make the play. That opens a window for the completion.

Mahomes’ escapes happened when the EDGE rushers decided to attack upfield and compromised the integrity of their rush lanes, giving him room to extend the play and find his receivers. That’s something to keep an eye on against Caleb Williams.

There were also a few execution errors. This is a great call by MM. He sends the outside corner on a blitz, rotates the nickel into the deep-safety role, spins Okada around, and drops Julian Love into coverage. The safety identifies the target and drives downhill, but misses the tackle, allowing the Chiefs to turn the play into a very manageable fourth-down situation.

Late in the game, the defense lost focus on a few plays. Here, Mahomes was in a bad situation, but Seattle allowed the completion, missed two tackles, and gave up a solid gain.

Final Thoughts

The 20–3 win over Kansas City was important for Seattle in more ways than one. After losses to Washington and Denver, the team needed to respond against a quality opponent and regain some confidence. The defense did exactly that in convincing fashion, the rushing attack improved as the game went on, and the offensive line showed some much-needed progress.

That doesn’t mean every problem has disappeared. The red-zone struggles are still costing the Seahawks points, and Darnold needs to show that he can avoid unnecessary mistakes. Against a more efficient opponent, those issues could turn a comfortable win into a painful loss.

The next matchup, against the Chicago Bears, will be another important test. Ben Johnson’s team has offensive talent and a quarterback capable of creating problems, while Mike Macdonald will have another opportunity to show how his defense adjusts to a different offense.

It will be another chance to play in prime time and show that the win over Kansas City wasn’t a one-off.

The division is still in the distance, but Seattle is back in the fight.

Go Hawks!

item.title: Examining Mizzou’s roster turnover coming out of the bye week
item.description: How have Mizzou’s arrivals and departures performed so far?
item.content:encoded:
Yearly roster turnover yearly can make it tough to keep up with exactly who is on the roster year-over-year, who’s left, and how those players are performing. As for Mizzou, it saw 30 incoming transfers and 26 departures prior to the beginning of the 2026 season.

Mizzou sits at 5-2, and No. 23 in the nation ahead of traveling to Arkansas on Halloween. Coming out of the bye week, here’s how the portal class and departures have performed so far this season:

Arrivals

Austin Simmons (From Mississippi): Simmons has been the upgrade the Tigers’ offense has needed in comparison to 2025. As noted on Sunday, he has 14 completions of 20-plus yards. He’s fourth in the SEC in passing yards (1,773) with the sixth-most passing touchdowns (14). The southpaw has risen up NFL Draft boards with his arm talent.

Cayden Lee (From Mississippi): Helping elevate Mizzou’s receiving game to another level, Lee is Simmons’ No. 1 go-to target, especially on third down, while being one of the most productive receivers in the nation. His 678 receiving yards rank 14th in the nation and are 2nd in the SEC. 81% of his snaps have come from the slot, and he is on track for a career year as a senior.

Robert Woodyard Jr. (From Auburn): Woodyard has paired nicely alongside Nicholas Rodriguez as the Tigers’ starting middle linebackers. He ranks second on the team in tackles (34) with 2.5 for a loss and a crucial interception against Kansas. Filling in the STAR, Kensley Louidor-Faustin has been great against the run game (Especially against Florida). He has an 80.4 PFF run defense grade and a 70.1 tackling grade. Along with a pair of pressures, he has 27 tackles and 5.0 for a loss.

Chris Graves Jr. (From Mississippi): No one has played more snaps at cornerback for Mizzou than Graves (384) this season. On the season so far, he has 13 tackles and 5 pass breakups. In coverage, he’s been targeted 26 times per PFF, allowing 12 receptions for 179 and a 94.9 NFL passer rating. Until the Ole Miss game, he was outstanding in not giving up any scores, but surrendered his first two of his collegiate career in a 31-3 loss. Besides that, he’s been relatively solid for the Tigers as their No. 1 cornerback.

Sione Laulea (From Oregon): As for MU’s No. 2 cornerback, he’s been targeted 36 times in coverage, giving up 19 receptions and 3 scores. He has 5 pass breakups and a cool interception in Lawrence. Laulea also ranks fourth in tackles with 29, including a TFL.

Luke Work (From Mississippi State): After very little experience at right tackle in the past two years for Work, the results have been about what you’ve expected as he’s filled in for the injured Josh Atkins. He’s allowed the most pressures on the team (12) by seven, tied for the second-most penalties (4), while allowing two of the team’s 5 sacks on the year.

Donta Simpson Jr. (From Miami-FL): As noted on Sunday, he ranks second on the team in pressures (19.0) and sacks (5.0). This is paired with 11 tackles, 5.5 for a loss, providing a boost to the Tigers’ interior defensive line.

Elijah Dotson (From Michigan): Dotson was one of the immediate standouts for the Tigers in week one, while collecting an interception in the end zone against Texas A&M. He’s seen an increased usage since his freshman year at Michigan. His defensive snaps count is up from 94 to 360, while collecting 28 tackles, one for a loss. He’s been all over the defense with 198 snaps at free safety, 109 in the box, 48 in the slot, and 4 along the defensive line. 

Jahlil Florence (Oregon): MU’s No. 3 cornerback. After missing time due to injury in 2024 and 25, he’s up to 180 defensive snaps in 2026. Impressively, he’s been targeted 21 times, but has allowed just 5 receptions and a 19.7 NFL passer rating. He also collected a pick against Kansas.

Naeshaun Montgomery (From Florida): Montgomery ranks third on the team in receiving with 136 yards on 10 receptions. In the return game, he’s been electric with 137 yards and a score on a punt return. In the kick return game, he has 184 yards on 6 returns.

Bruno Reus (From Florida State): Reus has been a solid punter for the Tigers since arriving from Tallahassee. He’s down 14 punts inside the 20, while just one has been returned. Also from FSU, Jaden Jones has been Mizzou’s fourth pass rusher. A bulk of his production came in the absence of Darris Smith and Langden Kitchen, where 85 of his 133 snaps have came. So far on his season, he has 4 tackles and 3 pressures.

Caleb Goodie Sr. (From Cincinnati): As a deep threat receiver, Goodie has 4 receptions, for 94 yards and a score. His average depth of target (23.6) surpasses anyone on the team by 7.3 yards. Kenric Lanier (From Minnesota) has a pair of receptions for 29 yards.

Xai’Shaun Edwards (From Houston Christian): Edwards has seen his snaps decrease the past few games offensively. But he’s Mizzou’s second-leading rusher with 132 yards on 39 carries and a score.

Mark Hensley (From Northern Illinois): After playing 46 snaps per game for the Huskies in 2025, Hensley has just logged 76 defensive snaps in 2026, with 43 coming over the past three games. He’s collected 6 tackles and a press break this season. Hensley has also appeared in 26 field goal snaps.

Kamauryn Morgan (From Baylor): 30 of Morgan’s 44 defensive snaps came against Mississippi State and Florida. On the year, he has 2 tackles and a pressure.

Malik Bryant (From Miami-FL): Bryant has appeared in 44 defensive snaps for Missouri this season, tallying 4 pressures, 2 tackles, and 0.5 sacks. Also, coming from South Beach, linebacker Bobby Washington Jr. has tallied 105 special teams snaps. Against Texas A&M, he was used as a quarterback spy, where six of his 20 defensive snaps of the season came. 

Zach Owens (From Mississippi State): Owens played in 500-plus snaps in Starkville a season ago, but is a depth piece at guard. After 41 snaps against Arkansas-Pine Bluff, he’s played just two offensive snaps since.

Cavan Tuley (From Houston): 18 of Tuley’s 38 defensive snaps came against Mississippi State. On the year, he has 4 tackles and 0.5 sacks.

Malei Fonoti (Montana): Fonoti’s season unfortunately ended with an ACL injury after week one. He carried the ball 3 times against UAPB for 18 yards. JaDon Blair (From Notre Dame) has played just 9 snaps this season, all coming against UAPB. Nick Evers (From UConn) went 1-of-2 for 18 yards in that game.

Has not made an appearance: Colin Sorensen (Charleston Southern), CJ May (Louisville), Will Kemma (Kansas State), Mark Shenouda (Tennessee State), Josh Atkins (Arizona State – Injured).

Departures

Beau Pribula (To Virginia): After a 2-0 start, the Cavaliers sit at 4-4. Pribula has thrown for 1,369 yards, 13 touchdowns and 2 picks so far this season. He improved on his deep passing, with 12 completions of 20-plus yards.

Damon Wilson II (To Miami-FL): Through seven games, on the No. 1 team in the nation, Wilson has 26 pressures and 3.5 sacks. That pressure total leads the Hurricanes.

Johnny Williams IV (To North Texas): Williams has been solid as the Mean Green’s starting left tackle. He has an 81.1 PFF pass-blocking grade, while allowing just 6 pressures and 2 sacks all season. He’s blocking for Brendon Haygood, who is the team’s second-leading rusher with 164 yards and 2 scores. Henry Fenuku joined them in Denton and has played just 8 offensive snaps.

Marvin Burks (To Wisconsin): Burks has 16 tackles and 2 interceptions for the Badgers, both coming against UCLA. 

Marquis Johnson (To Mississippi State): Johnson has found a role in Jeff Lebby’s veer-and-shoot offense. He’s the Bulldogs’ third-leading receiver with 259 yards on 18 receptions.

Daniel Blood (To Washington State): Blood followed Kirby Moore to Washington State, where he’s the Cougars second-leading receiver with 309 yards, 30 receptions, and a score.

Mose Phillips III (To Oklahoma State): Phillips unfortunately saw his season come to an end with a shoulder injury against UCF. After 149 snaps for the Tigers in 2025, he appeared in 199 snaps in five games for the Cowboys, collecting 23 tackles and an interception.

Tavorus Jones (To UTEP): This season, Jones is the Miners’ second-leading rusher with 261 yards on 58 attempts. He’s also added 45 receiving yards on 9 receptions.

Nate Johnson (To Auburn): Johnson has 11 tackles, 1 sack, and 3 pressures for Auburn.

Justin Bodford (To Middle Tennessee State): Bodford has 7 tackles, 2 sacks and 3 pressures in his first season in Murfreesboro.

Javion Hilson (To Virginia Tech): Hilson has played sporadically for the Hokies. In 86 defensive snaps, he has 6 tackles, 1.5 for loss and 2 pressures. 

Josh Manning (To Kansas State): Manning is the Wildcats third-leading receiver with 254 yards and 2 scores. Keiton Jones started at right guard in the first three weeks for the Wildcats. He allowed just 2 pressures in 107 offensive snaps.

Caleb Flagg (To UCF): Flagg has 13 tackles for the Knights this season.

Marquise Davis (To Louisville): Playing behind a talented backfield of Isaac Browns and Keyjuan Brown, Davis has accumulated 144 yards and 3 scores for the Cardinals.

Jayven Richardson (To Colorado): Richardson has appeared in just 8 offensive snaps for the Buffaloes.

Robert Meyer (To UC Davis): This season, Meyer is 6-for-9 on field goals, but perfect inside the 40.

Bralen Henderson and Dakotah Terrell – Not listed on a current team.

Has not made an appearance: Shamar McNeil (Akron), Jaylen Early (Texas State), Mark Manfred III (Kentucky), Brandon Solis (Kansas), James Madison II (UTSA).

item.title: Saints vs. Steelers: Week 7 Game MVP
item.description: Chase Young is showcasing why he was voted as a captain for the Saints and Granderson is right there with him
item.content:encoded:
Another disappointing finish for the New Orleans Saints, but even amid the struggles, one player is showing up consistently. Without his presence in Paris, this game probably would have gotten out of hand quickly.

Chase Young is the MVP of this game and, so far, of the season. Young was voted a captain to begin the season, and he is living up to that standard. On Sunday, Young finished the game with two tackles (one solo and one assisted), 1.5 sacks, and one tackle for loss.

Even on the plays he did not make, his presence on the edge was felt, as he was stressing the Steelers’ offensive tackles on every play. According to PFF, Chase Young has the second-best pass-rush grade in the NFL.

An honorable mention would be Carl Granderson. Granderson seems to be the complement to Chase Young, and against the Steelers, he finished with four total tackles, 1.5 sacks, and one tackle for loss.

Granderson has been developing over the past several seasons, and if he can continue this progression, it would help the Saints consider adding defensive help at other major positions of need.

Who was your game MVP? How are you feeling about this season so far? Share your thoughts and sound off in the comments below.

item.title: Detroit Lions tagged as ‘best fit’ for 4 trade deadline candidates
item.description: ESPN put a list of 25 NFL trade deadline candidates, and the Detroit Lions were best fits for four of them.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL trade deadline is just under two weeks away—Tuesday, November 10—and several trades have already been made. So ESPN insiders Jeremy Fowler and Matt Bowen put together a list of the top-25 candidates to get traded by the deadline. Interestingly, they also listed at least two teams that they view as the best team fits for a landing spot.

In their list of 25 traded candidates, the Detroit Lions were listed as one of the best fits for four of those candidates. Let’s go through them one-by-one.

Eagles CB Riq Woolen

It’s not surprising the Lions are being paired with a cornerback, given their struggles at that position this year. Although it is interesting to see the Lions have some recent success at cornerback after utilizing some rotation with the players they have.

The Eagles are 2-5 and will be without starting quarterback Jalen Hurts for the rest of the season. They definitely could be sellers at the trade deadline, and ESPN lists Woolen at a 35% likelihood of being traded.

He’s on a very manageable contract, with the acquiring team only responsible for a prorated amount of his $6 million base salary.

He would bring some height and length (6-foot-4) to the outside cornerback position, but his play hasn’t been as good as his best Seahawks days. This season alone, PFF credits him with 20 catches on 36 targets for 282 yards, 4 touchdowns—but he does have six passes defended and a forced fumble.

Here’s what Matt Bowen had to say about his play this year:

 “Woolen has the length and long speed at 6-foot-4 to help a defense majoring in man coverage and two-deep zone. The tackling and eye discipline could improve, but Woolen is a disruptor on the perimeter.”

Chargers CB Donte Jackson

The Chargers are the only winless team remaining, and with the Rams, Ravens, Patriots, 49ers, Chiefs, and Broncos still on the schedule, their season is already toast.

Jackson will be 31 next month, but he’s had an illustrious NFL career. Over nine years, he’s started 109 games, tallied 23 interceptions, and 68 passes defended. He was a captain for several years with the Panthers, so he’s high-character, as well.

Financially, this is another easy one. It’s the same as Woolen: all the acquiring team would need is to fit a prorated amount of Jackson’s $6 million salary.

Here’s Bowen’s analysis:

“With his backfield vision and short-area closing speed, Jackson fits best as a zone corner. He’s a top-down defender with route awareness who can create on-the-ball production”

Bengals EDGE Shemar Stewart

While the Bengals are far from sellers at 4-2 on the season, they have been barely playing Stewart, who was the team’s 17th overall pick just last year. Stewart has played in just 17 snaps this season.

Despite that, I think it’s unlikely Cincinnati moves on from Stewart this early in his career. He missed nearly all of training camp with a leg injury, and that was part of Zac Taylor’s explanation for having Stewart inactive this past week.

“He’s doing all the right things. He’s getting better every week. (He missed) training camp for the most part. So, to get him back, I think he’s been doing a great job of practicing. We’re just in a really tough spot with our inactives right now. Sometimes we’re really healthy. Sometimes we’re beat up at a position where we need another guy up. So, unfortunately, we just had to pull from the d-line, and it’s a really deep d-line group, and it’s really difficult to choose who’s going to be inactive there.”

But in the unlikely situation he’s on the block, he is a very good fit in Detroit. He’s long, strong, and extremely physical.

Saints G Cesar Ruiz

This is just a bizarre one. Ruiz could very well be on the block for a 2-5 Saints team, but it’s hard to imagine the Lions getting involved for a guard. Not only has Ruiz played right guard for almost his entire NFL career—where Lions’ second-year player Tate Ratledge is holding things down just fine—but the Lions have also been getting really solid play out of Christian Mahogany at left guard. And they have a good backup option in Juice Scruggs.

Not sure what ESPN is thinking with this one. It ain’t happening.
